title: Building Systems, Not Just Brands
excerpt: Why we focus on creating frameworks and systems rather than one-off solutions. The case for investing in infrastructure over individual outputs.
body:
There's a particular kind of brand failure that nobody talks about honestly. The logo is great. The colour palette is considered. The typography is tight. The brand guidelines document is 80 pages of well-designed nothing. And six months later, the whole thing is dead in the water.

Not because the brand was bad. Because there was nothing holding it up.

## Brand Without Infrastructure Is Just Decoration

I worked with a company — sharp founders, genuinely interesting product — who came to us after spending a significant sum on a rebrand from a well-regarded agency. The deliverables were excellent. Beautifully crafted. The problem was simple: nobody inside the organisation had any idea how to use them.

Customer comms still sounded like a law firm. Sales decks were assembled by whoever had time, which meant twelve different visual treatments across the team. The Instagram was being managed by whoever grabbed the login that week. Within nine months, the brand had effectively reverted to what it was before — just with a nicer logo.

The agency had built a face. Nobody had built the body.

## What System Actually Means

When I say system, I mean the operational scaffolding that makes a brand reproduce itself consistently without requiring constant creative intervention. That means a few things.

First, it means language. Not a tone-of-voice document with adjectives and vague guidance. I mean actual copy frameworks: sentence structures, vocabulary choices, what you don't say and why. Decisions a junior team member can execute correctly without calling a creative director.

Second, it means decision-making templates. When a new use case emerges — a product announcement, a collab, an internal comms piece — what's the process? Most brands have no answer to this. The answer is usually: whoever has the most seniority in the room that day. That's not a system. That's chaos with plausible deniability.

Third, it means feedback loops. How does the brand learn? What gets reviewed, by whom, on what cadence? The brands I've seen sustain themselves over time have internal review rhythms. They catch drift early.

## The Creative Director's Real Job

I've come to think the most important thing a creative director does isn't make things. It's make making possible. You're designing a process, not just an output.

That sounds abstract, so here's the concrete version: if a client can't continue operating the brand we designed without us, we've failed. Not partially failed. Fundamentally failed. We've made them dependent on a service relationship instead of genuinely building their capability.

The best brand work I've done has always included documentation that felt almost embarrassingly thorough — decisions explained, options outlined, rationale articulated. Not because clients need hand-holding, but because brands live inside organisations for years, and organisations change. The new CMO who joins eighteen months later needs to be able to read the system and understand not just what it is, but why.

## Brand Is Infrastructure

The word infrastructure is useful because it implies something load-bearing. You don't see infrastructure unless something goes wrong. Roads, plumbing, electrical systems — they're invisible when they work, catastrophically visible when they don't.

Brand should work the same way. When the system is right, every piece of communication that comes out of an organisation carries the brand correctly, automatically, without heroic effort. The brand is load-bearing. It's holding something up.

When the system is wrong — or absent — every piece of communication requires a decision. Every decision requires effort. Every effort is a tax on the organisation. Most brands are paying that tax constantly and calling it normal.

It isn't normal. It's a design failure.

The work isn't to make something beautiful and hand it over. The work is to build something that works when you're not watching.

title: Why I Built My Portfolio on a BlackBerry OS
excerpt: The thinking behind our retro device interface. Nostalgia as a design tool, and why constraint breeds creativity.
body:
The most common reaction when people land on this portfolio is a slight pause. Sometimes confusion. Then, if I'm doing my job, curiosity.

That pause is the whole point.

## This Isn't Nostalgia

Let me be direct about something. This is not a design decision rooted in nostalgia. I don't have particular fondness for the BlackBerry Bold era. I didn't carry one in 2008 with some romantic attachment to physical keyboards and BBM. This isn't about looking back.

It's about what the BlackBerry represented as a design philosophy, and why that philosophy is more relevant now than it was then.

The BlackBerry was a machine that made you work. Small screen. Physical keyboard. No app ecosystem to escape into. It shipped with constraints so severe that using it required genuine attention — you couldn't zone out, you couldn't swipe endlessly, you couldn't accidentally consume three hours of content. The friction was the feature.

And people loved it. Not despite the friction. Because of it.

## What Friction Does

We've spent fifteen years designing friction out of digital experiences. Every tap saved, every scroll made smoother, every decision pre-made so the user doesn't have to think. The result is interfaces so frictionless that nothing sticks. People move through them without being touched.

That's fine for most products. For a creative portfolio, it's fatal.

A portfolio is a trust document. It's supposed to tell you something about how someone thinks — not just what they've made, but how they approach problems, what they value, what they'd be like to work with. A scroll-through landing page with a big reel and some case study thumbnails tells you almost nothing. It's designed to remove friction, which means it's designed to remove the experience of actually encountering someone.

When you navigate this site — when you open an app, press a button, move between screens — you're experiencing a designed environment. Every decision in it was made deliberately. The constraints aren't limitations. They're the argument.

## The Obvious Objection

Yes, I know. I've heard it. "Isn't this just aesthetic? A design trick? You're still just a portfolio with a quirky wrapper."

No.

The wrapper is the work. The medium is the message — that's not a cliché, it's a design principle. When I ship a portfolio that makes you navigate a BB OS to see case studies, I'm making a statement about how I think about interaction, about constraint, about the relationship between form and content. You're not reading my design philosophy. You're experiencing it.

That's a different thing entirely.

If you came here and thought: "this is just showing off" — that's a valid read. But consider the alternative. You could have arrived at a white-background grid with a 12-second reel and a contact form. Would you have learned anything? Would you have felt anything? Would you have formed any opinion about what it might actually be like to work with me?

## Constraint As Position

Every meaningful creative position involves choosing what you won't do as deliberately as what you will. Most portfolios try to appeal to everyone — clean, neutral, professional, inoffensive. Which means they don't actually appeal to anyone in particular.

This portfolio is not for everyone. It will confuse some people. Some will bounce immediately. Good. Those aren't my people.

The people who pause, look around, figure out how it works, and feel something — those are. The friction is a filter. The design is a selection mechanism.

Constraint doesn't limit expression. In the right hands, it defines it.

The BlackBerry OS isn't the point. The willingness to make a position is the point. Everything else follows from that.

title: Content Velocity
excerpt: Balancing speed and craft in 2025. How we structure production to maintain quality at scale without burning out.
body:
The quality-versus-quantity debate is the wrong question. I've sat through versions of this argument at every type of brand I've worked with — the startup that wants to post daily and wonders why everything feels thin, the heritage brand that agonises over every piece and wonders why nobody's paying attention. Both are losing. Neither is asking the right question.

The right question is: how fast are you learning?

## The Feedback Loop Is the Point

Content velocity isn't about output rate. It's about the cadence of your learning cycle. Volume without reflection is noise — you're producing things that go nowhere and teaching yourself nothing. Perfection without iteration is ego — you're spending enormous energy on individual pieces while the market moves and your assumptions calcify.

What actually matters is the loop: make something, put it out, observe what happens, adjust, repeat. The faster and tighter that loop, the faster you get better. The slower and looser it is, the more you're just guessing at scale.

Most brands break this loop in two predictable ways.

## The Two Failure Modes

The first is moving too fast in the wrong dimension. They produce at high volume — daily posts, constant stories, weekly drops — but they're not reviewing anything. Nobody's asking: what performed? What didn't? Why? What did we learn about our audience this month? The content machine is running but it's not connected to anything. It's burning budget and attention without generating intelligence.

The second is moving too slow in the wrong dimension. They agonise over single pieces. Approval chains, revision cycles, committee sign-off. By the time something goes out, the conversation has moved. And because they've invested so much in each piece, they're reluctant to measure it honestly — if this piece fails, months of effort fail with it. So they don't measure it properly. The feedback loop is broken by the weight of what's riding on it.

Both modes are painful. One produces quantity that doesn't compound. The other produces quality that doesn't iterate.

## What Good Velocity Looks Like

The cadence that actually works is specific. Here's a breakdown of what I run with clients who are getting it right.

Weekly: one substantial piece — written, video, audio, whatever the format is — that requires real thought and takes a genuine position. Not a hot take. An actual perspective that could only come from you, with reasoning behind it. This is the piece you're genuinely proud of.

Three times weekly: reactive or contextual content. Shorter form. Responding to what's happening in the space, amplifying the substantial piece, staying present without requiring the same investment. Fast to make, fast to review.

Monthly: a proper review. What moved? What didn't? What assumption did you make that turned out to be wrong? What did your audience tell you — explicitly or implicitly — that you need to incorporate? This is the most important session of the month and most brands skip it entirely.

The ratio matters. One high-effort piece surrounded by lower-effort presence work, all reviewed against real data on a monthly cycle. It's not glamorous. It works.

## Speed Is Not the Enemy

There's a cultural bias in creative work toward slowness as a signal of quality. The idea that if it was made quickly, it must be cheap. This is wrong and it's worth being direct about it.

Speed — when applied to the right things — is how you get better. The fastest way to improve is to make things, see how they land, and adjust. The brands I've watched build real creative authority over the last few years are the ones that moved with conviction — not recklessly, not without craft, but without the paralysis that comes from treating every output like it defines you.

Content velocity, properly understood, is a learning strategy. It's not about how much you make. It's about how much you learn per unit of time. Optimise for that, and the quality follows.

title: The Anti-Portfolio
excerpt: Work we turned down, and why. Sometimes the most important decisions are about what you don't do.
body:
Every portfolio is constructed. That's obvious, but it's worth saying out loud because the implications aren't always followed through. If you've made selections, you've made omissions. And if the omissions weren't deliberate, you've made unconscious choices that reveal something about you — just not necessarily what you intended.

I've thought a lot about what HandToMouse doesn't show. Here's the honest version.

## What We Leave Out

We don't show work that we executed but didn't direct. There's a category of project — good money, interesting client — where you're brought in to make something specific happen, and the strategic decisions were already made by someone else. The work might be technically excellent. We still don't include it. Because the portfolio is supposed to demonstrate thinking, not technical execution, and including that work would be dishonest about what we contributed.

We don't show work for clients we couldn't genuinely align with. I've taken projects early in this business that I knew were compromises — a brief that didn't fit, a client whose values were sideways to mine, a category I found dull. Some of that work is good on the surface. It's still not in the book. Because if you're trying to attract clients who are right for you, showing work done for clients who weren't right for you is actively counterproductive. You signal the wrong thing.

We don't show trend-chasing work. Any creative business that's been operating for a few years has done at least some work that felt current at the time and looks dated fast. The portfolio should reflect where you're going, not where the market was two years ago.

## The Edit Is the Argument

Here's what most creative portfolios get wrong: they're additive. More case studies, more categories covered, more range demonstrated. The logic is: cover more ground, reduce the chance of missing a client. This is wrong.

A portfolio that tries to appeal to everyone appeals to no one in particular. It creates a generic impression. And generic impressions don't generate the kind of trust that leads to good work, because the client has no idea what they're actually buying. They see capability, not perspective.

A tighter portfolio — fewer pieces, more deliberate — is a trust signal. It says: we chose these. We chose them for a reason. We have a point of view on what good work is, and we're prepared to stand behind it. That's a different kind of pitch than "here are all the things we've made."

When a potential client sees a portfolio and asks "why do you only show X type of work?" — that's a great question. It opens a conversation about perspective and positioning. That conversation leads to better briefs, better work, better relationships. The question never gets asked from a portfolio that shows everything.

## What Saying No Teaches You

The anti-portfolio — the work declined, the projects left off — is also a record of the decisions that shaped the business. Every no is a position. Every omission is a vote for what you stand for.

I've turned down significant project value to stay on the right side of this. Work in categories that would have diluted the positioning. Clients whose attitude toward the creative process would have produced bad work and bad case studies. Projects where the brief was so locked down there was no room to make anything worth showing.

Those decisions cost real money in the short term. In the medium term, they're the reason the portfolio holds together as a coherent statement rather than a collection of whatever happened to come through the door.

The anti-portfolio is the edit. The edit is what makes the work legible. Without it, you don't have a portfolio. You have an archive.

Archives are for historians. Portfolios are for people who want to work with you.

title: Working With Creators
excerpt: The shift from influencer marketing to genuine creator partnerships. What works, what doesn't, and where we see this going.
body:
Most brands fundamentally misunderstand what they're buying when they commission a creator. They want the audience without respecting the voice that built it. That's the mistake, and it explains why most creator partnerships are mediocre at best and brand-damaging at worst.

Let me be specific about where this goes wrong.

## The Media Buy Mindset

The dominant model in brand-creator relationships is still, essentially, a media buy. The brand identifies a creator with the right audience demographics. They calculate the CPM. They make an offer. They send a brief. The brief specifies what to say, how to say it, which products to feature, what claims to make, which hashtags to include. The creator executes. The content goes out.

This model produces content that every audience can smell immediately. It looks like the creator's content, uses the creator's format, but it reads like a press release that someone dressed up in casual language. The audience knows. They've always known. And over time, their trust in that creator erodes — which means the brand has actively destroyed the asset it was trying to leverage.

You cannot separate the audience from the voice that built it. Audiences don't follow accounts. They follow people — or the idea of people — because of how that person thinks, what they notice, how they express things. The moment you override that voice with a brand brief, you've broken the thing you came for.

## Brief for Outcomes, Not Executions

The fix is a different kind of brief. Most brand briefs specify execution: say this, show this, include this call to action, hit these talking points. A brief that actually works specifies outcomes: we want our audience to understand that this product solves X problem. We want it to feel like a natural part of your content, not a departure from it. Here's context about the product. Here's what we care about. Make the thing.

This is uncomfortable for brands because it requires genuine relinquishment of control. Most brand managers have spent careers being accountable for messaging consistency and legal compliance. The idea of handing a brief to a third party with "make the thing" is terrifying. It shouldn't be, but it is.

The brands that are good at this — the ones whose creator partnerships actually generate trust and conversion — have made a cultural decision to treat creators as creative partners, not production vendors. The brief is a starting point for a conversation, not a spec sheet.

## Trust Is the Product

When a creator partnership works, what you're actually distributing is trust. The creator's audience trusts them. If the creator's endorsement is genuine, some of that trust transfers. That transfer is the value.

This only happens if the creator's recommendation is credible. And credibility only exists if the creator had a genuine experience and genuine latitude to express it. You can't manufacture credibility from outside. You can only create the conditions for it.

So the question I ask every brand I work with on creator strategy is: do you actually trust this creator's judgment about how to present your product to their audience? If the answer is no — if you need to approve every word before it goes out — then you've already decided you don't want a creator partnership. You want a media buy. Those are different things with different outcomes.

## The Difference That Matters

A sponsored post is a transaction. A creator partnership is a collaboration. They produce different things.

A sponsored post produces content. Creator partnerships, done right, produce credibility — and over time, that credibility compounds. The creator becomes someone who genuinely uses and believes in the product, which means their future content — not paid, not contracted — carries that association too. That's an asset you can't buy. You can only earn it.

Most brands are choosing the transaction because it's legible, controllable, and feels safe. It's none of those things. The CPM math works. The trust math doesn't.

If you want to work with creators, the first question isn't: which creator has the right audience? It's: are we prepared to actually collaborate? If the answer is no, save everyone's time and buy a display ad instead. At least that's honest.
